standard.title: Organise primary and secondary sources
standard.description: locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4S02 (Collect information from source ranges): Students collect and record information from provided sources including timelines, maps and models. Students have practised sorting and recording data at Year 4 level.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, collect and organise information and data from a range of primary and secondary sources in multiple formats, selecting appropriate organisational tools and applying cartographic and graphing conventions.

nodes.label: Primary vs secondary sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between primary and secondary sources, give examples of each relevant to HASS contexts, and explain the value of each type for different inquiry purposes.
nodes.minimum_width: Define primary and secondary sources and give one example of each from a HASS context.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish between primary sources (e.g. maps, diaries, official documents, photographs, artefacts, newspapers of the day, oral histories, fieldwork observations) and secondary sources (e.g. books, internet articles, reports), and explain when each type is most useful for an inquiry.
wider: Investigate a historical event using both a primary source and a secondary source on the same topic, and compare what each reveals and what it omits

Explore how digital technologies have changed the availability of primary sources — consider how sources like social media posts, government datasets and satellite imagery function as primary sources for contemporary investigations
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the primary/secondary distinction, students cannot evaluate the provenance or reliability of sources in subsequent nodes, and cannot apply the source evaluation skills in AC9HS5S04. This distinction is the prerequisite for purposeful source work across Year 5.

response_modes.reason: Students often confuse primary and secondary sources — and errors in applying this distinction flow through all source evaluation work. Use repeated classification practice across varied examples to build fluency.

success_criteria: Students correctly classify at least three examples as primary or secondary sources.
Students explain why each type of source is useful for a specific inquiry purpose.

nodes.label: Collecting and organising using graphic tools
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can collect and organise information and data using a range of digital and non-digital graphic organisers, selecting the tool appropriate to the purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Use one graphic organiser (e.g. flow chart, Venn diagram, timeline) to organise information for an inquiry purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Select and use appropriate graphic organisers (flow charts, consequence wheels, futures timelines, Venn diagrams, decision-making matrices, bibliography templates) to organise information, explaining why each tool suits the purpose.
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of two different graphic organisers for the same data and justify which is more useful for the inquiry purpose
Design a custom graphic organiser for a specific inquiry task and explain the design decisions that make it fit for purpose

response_modes.reason: Students need a varied toolkit of graphic organisers and the judgment to select the right one. Build repertoire by practising with multiple tool types rather than mastering one deeply.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The elaborations name six distinct organiser types — each has different analytical affordances. Building a genuine toolkit and selection judgment is a transferable inquiry skill with significant breadth potential.
success_criteria: Students use at least one graphic organiser to organise information for an inquiry purpose.
Students explain why the chosen organiser is appropriate for the information and purpose.

nodes.label: Constructing maps, timelines, tables and graphs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct timelines, maps, tables and graphs using appropriate digital applications and conventions, to display information and data.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct one map, timeline, table or graph using appropriate conventions to display data.
nodes.typical_width: Construct timelines, maps, tables and graphs using appropriate digital applications and cartographic conventions (border, source, scale, legend, title, north point) to display data relevant to HASS investigations such as movement of peoples, population growth, key event sequences, and cultural group distributions.
wider: Create a digital map using a geospatial tool (e.g. Google Maps, ArcGIS Online) to display HASS data, applying all cartographic conventions correctly
Compare a map, graph and timeline of the same dataset and evaluate how each display choice shapes what the viewer understands about the data

response_modes.reason: Cartographic and graphing conventions are precise skills that require practice — errors in conventions (missing north point, unlabelled axis) undermine the communication of findings. Fluency matters here.

success_criteria: Students construct at least one map, timeline, table or graph displaying HASS data.
Students apply relevant conventions correctly (e.g. title, legend, scale for maps; labelled axes for graphs).

nodes.label: Integrating multiple sources and formats
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate, collect and organise information from multiple primary and secondary sources in a range of formats, selecting appropriate organisational tools and conventions for the inquiry purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Collect information from at least two source types (one primary, one secondary) and organise it using appropriate tools for the inquiry purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Locate, collect and organise information and data from a range of primary and secondary sources in multiple formats (including geospatial tools, surveys, digital and non-digital sources), selecting appropriate organisational tools and applying relevant conventions.
wider: Conduct fieldwork or a survey to gather primary data, then organise and integrate this data with secondary source findings to produce a multi-source investigation
Evaluate the completeness of a source collection for an inquiry — identify what types of sources are missing and explain how adding them would improve the investigation

response_modes.reason: The integration challenge is coordinating multiple source types and formats into a coherent organised collection — students need to make deliberate decisions about which tool organises which information and why.

success_criteria: Students collect information from at least one primary and one secondary source.
Students organise collected information using an appropriate tool and apply conventions correctly.
Students explain why they selected the organisational tools and formats they used.
